rationale: A wins because it separates four real stories by protagonist: product mechanism, regulator, paying owner, and clinic. Its strongest line, “The sensors are in the cover. Knowing your blood oxygen costs the top subscription tier,” is a clean consumer-tech conflict with proof requirements attached. B has useful material, but “Beds are becoming health sensors, one mattress cover at a time” is a one-company trend trying to borrow altitude it has not earned, and “For athletes chasing recovery data” leans on audience assumption more than supplied evidence.
gaps_in_A: “detects snoring or a low SpO2 reading overnight and changes its own temperature in response” may overstate causality; the update says the product tracks those signals and adjusts temperature automatically, but not exactly what triggers what.
“whether its data means anything” is sharper than the facts can fully support until the clinic study design, endpoints, and independence are available.
The first angle should more plainly warn that the closed-loop story collapses if temperature adjustment is not specifically tied to snoring or SpO2 events.
gaps_in_B: “a live clinical study with an unnamed sleep clinic” contradicts the update, which says the clinic is named. That is a needless factual stumble.
“Beds are becoming health sensors, one mattress cover at a time” is padded category wallpaper; the set admits “there's no broader supplied signal beyond it” but keeps the trend angle anyway.

“For athletes chasing recovery data” assumes athletes would treat SpO2 and snoring as a useful recovery metric; the update only says Eight Sleep markets to athletes and biohackers, not that they want or use this data.

“premiumization of health monitoring” and “health-equity reporter” are a bit grand for a several-thousand-dollar smart mattress subscription gate unless there is access data or affected-population proof.
